contentful:
Contentful stores one value per locale in every localizable field, so the quickest route today is a short script: read the fields in your default locale, translate them with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) and write them back into the target locale.

1. Add the target languages under *Settings → Locales* and mark the fields that need translating as *localizable* in the content model.
2. Create a Content Management API token, and get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
3. With the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) and the Contentful Management SDK, read the entries you want, send the text and rich text fields to Supertext in one job, and save the results in the target locale as drafts.
4. Review the drafts in the entry editor (switch the locale in the sidebar) and publish.

Smaller jobs: export a few entries with `contentful space export`, translate the texts in the JSON with the SDK, and import them again with `contentful space import`.
sanity:
In Sanity, translations live either in a document per language (document internationalization) or in a field per language (internationalized arrays). Either way, a script with the Sanity client and the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) translates them today.

1. Set up the languages in your schema, with `@sanity/document-internationalization` or `sanity-plugin-internationalized-array`.
2. Create a Sanity API token with write access, and get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
3. Query the documents in the source language with GROQ, send the string and Portable Text fields to Supertext, and write the translations as drafts: a new language document, or the matching array entry.
4. Review the drafts in Sanity Studio and publish.

Portable Text is JSON: translate the text of each span and keep the marks and keys, so links and styles survive.
sitecore:
Sitecore keeps a version of each item per language. Today you can export the field values of a language, translate the file with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and import it again, or translate items through the API with the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk).

1. Add the target language under *System → Languages* and create the language versions you need.
2. On Sitecore XP/XM, export the source texts with *Control Panel → Globalization → Export languages*. On XM Cloud, read the items through the Authoring and Management GraphQL API.
3. Translate the exported file with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or send the field values to Supertext with the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk).
4. Import the translated file with *Import languages*, or write the values into the target language versions, then review them in the Content Editor or Pages and publish.

Keep shared and unversioned fields out of the export: only versioned fields differ per language.
rws-tridion:
In RWS Tridion Sites, translations are localized items in child publications of the BluePrint. Today you can translate them with a script on the Core Service or the Content Manager API and the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk).

1. Make sure each target language has its own publication in the BluePrint, below the source publication.
2. Read the components and pages to translate from the source publication through the API your Tridion team uses.
3. Send the text and rich text fields to Supertext with the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk) and get them back in the same structure.
4. Localize the items in the target publication, write the translated values and send them through your usual review and publish workflow.

Just a few pages? Copy the texts into a Word file, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and paste the results into the localized items.
opentext:
OpenText covers many products, from Content Server and Documentum to TeamSite and Experience Cloud. For documents the route today is the same everywhere: download the file, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) with the formatting kept, and add it back as a language version.

1. Download the Word, Excel or PowerPoint file, or export the page content as HTML.
2. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target languages. The translated file keeps the layout.
3. Upload the translation as a new document, or as a language variant or rendition, depending on how your repository manages languages.
4. Link it to the source document so updates to the original can be translated again.

Many documents a month? The OpenText APIs plus the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) automate the round trip; [talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact) about the setup.
plytix:
Plytix imports and exports products as spreadsheets, so the route today is a round trip: export the attributes to translate, translate the file with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), and import it into the attributes for each language.

1. Create an attribute per language for each text you translate (for example *Description DE* and *Description FR*), or use the language versions if your account has them.
2. Select the products, choose *Export* and include the SKU and the source-language text attributes, as Excel or CSV.
3. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com): the text columns are translated, and the SKUs and numbers stay as they are.
4. Import the translated file, map the columns to the target-language attributes, and check a few products before you update your channels.

For a catalogue that changes every week, a script with the Plytix API and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates only new and changed products.
salesforce-marketing-cloud:
Marketing Cloud emails are HTML, and HTML translates well: the tags, links and AMPscript stay as they are and only the text changes. Today you can translate an email with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and create a version per language in Content Builder.

1. Open the email in Content Builder and copy its HTML from the code view, or read the asset through the REST API.
2. Save the HTML as a file and translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or send it to Supertext with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).
3. Create a copy of the email for each language and paste in the translated HTML.
4. To send each subscriber the right language, use dynamic content blocks on a language attribute, or keep the texts in a data extension and pull them in with AMPscript.

Translate the subject line and preheader too: they are separate fields, not part of the HTML.
figma:
There is no Supertext plugin for Figma yet, but its texts are easy to take out and put back. Today you export the text layers, translate them with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and apply the translations to a copy of the frames.

1. Duplicate the frames or the page for each target language, so the original stays untouched.
2. Export the text layers with a localization plugin from the Figma Community that writes them to a spreadsheet or JSON, or read them through the Figma REST API.
3. Translate the file with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or the keyed texts with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).
4. Import the translations into the copies with the same plugin and check the layout: German and French run about 30% longer than English.

Use Auto layout on buttons and text boxes before you start: longer translations then resize the frame instead of overflowing.
atlassian-confluence:
Confluence exports pages to Word, and Word translates with the formatting kept. Today you can translate a page with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and publish it as its own page per language.

1. Decide where the languages live: a child page per language, or a separate space per language.
2. Open the page and choose *More actions (…) → Export → Export to Word*.
3. Upload the Word file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target languages.
4. Create the page in the target language and paste in the translated content, or use the Word import where your Confluence edition offers it. Link the language versions to each other at the top of the page.

Many pages, or pages that change often? A script with the Confluence REST API and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates the page storage format directly; in an AI assistant, the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) can translate a page you paste in.
madcap-flare:
A Flare project is a folder of XHTML topics, snippets and a table of contents, which is a format translators handle every day. Today you send the project files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and build the target-language output from the translated copy.

1. Make a copy of the project for each target language and set its language under *Project → Project Properties → Language*.
2. Collect the topics and snippets of the copy, or create a translation bundle with MadCap Lingo if you use it (XLIFF).
3. Send the files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) as an order and mention that they come from Flare; with terminology and earlier translations, repeated sentences are translated the same way.
4. Put the translated files back into the copy, build the targets and check the TOC, variables and cross-references.

Translate the variables and the skin texts too: they live outside the topics.
madcap-ixia-ccms:
IXIA CCMS manages DITA topics and maps, and DITA is XML that translation tools read reliably. Today you export the map with its topics for translation and send the package to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Create the target language versions for the map you want to translate.
2. Export the map and its topics (and the reusable content they reference) as a translation package of DITA XML files.
3. Send the package to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) as an order; only the text is translated, the elements, attributes and conrefs stay as they are.
4. Import the translated package into IXIA CCMS, check the language versions and publish the outputs.

Translate only what changed: unchanged topics keep their earlier translation, which saves time and cost.
paligo:
Paligo has a translation workflow built in: it exports your content as XLIFF and imports the translations again. Today you send those XLIFF files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Add the target languages to your Paligo instance.
2. Select the publication or topics and use *Export for translation* to create the XLIFF files.
3. Upload the XLIFF files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com). They come back in the same structure, with the tags and references intact.
4. Import the translations with *Import translation*, review them in Paligo and publish in the target languages.

Paligo only exports the parts that changed since the last translation, so later rounds are small.
quanos:
SCHEMA ST4 is built for translation: its translation export creates a package of the content to translate, and the import puts the translations back into the right nodes. Today you send that package to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Set up the target languages in ST4 if they are not there yet.
2. Start a translation export for the publication or nodes you need. ST4 includes only the content that is new or changed in the target language.
3. Send the export package (XML or XLIFF, depending on your configuration) to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) as an order.
4. Import the translated package into ST4, check the result in the target language and produce the publications.

Send us your ST4 terminology too: consistent terms matter most in technical documentation.
kovai-document360:
Document360 supports a knowledge base in several languages, with an article version per language. Today you export the articles, translate them with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and add them as the language version.

1. Add the target languages in the knowledge base settings.
2. Export the articles to translate: as an export file, or by reading them through the Document360 API.
3. Translate the Markdown or HTML with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or send the articles in one job with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).
4. Paste or import the translations into the target-language version of each article, review and publish.

Translate the category names and the knowledge base navigation too, so readers find their way in their language.
veeva-vault:
In Veeva Vault, a translation is usually its own document, linked to the source and reviewed in your normal workflow. Today you download the source file, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and add the translation to Vault.

1. Download the steady-state version of the source document (Word, Excel or PowerPoint).
2. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target languages. The layout stays as it is.
3. Create a document per language in Vault, with the language set, and link it to the source with the translation relationship your Vault uses.
4. Send the translations through review and approval as your quality process requires.

Regulated content needs a human review: [talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact) about specialist translators for medical and pharmaceutical texts.
articulate:
Both Articulate tools export their texts for translation and import them again, so a translated course keeps all its interactions. Today you translate those files with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. **Rise 360:** duplicate the course, then choose *Settings → Translations → Export XLIFF file*.
2. **Storyline 360:** choose *File → Translation → Export* and pick XLIFF or Word.
3. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target language.
4. Import the translated file into the duplicate (Rise: *Import translation*; Storyline: *File → Translation → Import*), then play the course through and check the text fits.

Replace the narration and the images with text in them separately: they are not part of the export.
microsoft-sharepoint:
SharePoint has multilingual pages built in: it creates a copy of a page per language and links the copies. Today you translate the content of those copies and the documents in your libraries with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Turn on *Enable pages and news to be translated into multiple languages* under *Site settings → Site information → Language settings*, and add the languages.
2. Open the page and choose *Translation → Create* for each language: SharePoint creates a copy to translate.
3. Translate the text of the page with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) in Copilot, and paste it into the copy. Documents (Word, Excel, PowerPoint): download, translate with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and upload the translation next to the original.
4. Publish the translated pages: visitors see the page in the language of their settings.

Many pages? The Microsoft Graph API and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translate pages and documents in bulk.
microsoft-365:
Word, Excel and PowerPoint files translate well as they are: [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) returns the file in the target language with the formatting, tables and slides kept. And in Copilot, the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) translates with Supertext directly.

1. Open the file in OneDrive, SharePoint or Teams and download it.
2. Upload it to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target languages and, if needed, a human review.
3. Upload the translation next to the original, with the language in the file name (for example *Report_DE.docx*).
4. For shorter texts, connect the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) to Copilot and ask it to translate with Supertext, using your terminology and style.

Keep the source in one file and the translations in their own files: one file per language is easier to update later.
google-docs:
Google Docs converts to Word and back without losing formatting. Today you download the document, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and open the translation as a new Google Doc.

1. Open the document and choose *File → Download → Microsoft Word (.docx)*. Sheets and Slides work the same way, as .xlsx and .pptx.
2. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and choose the target languages.
3. In Google Drive, choose *New → File upload* and open the translated file with Google Docs (it is converted automatically).
4. Share the translation with the same people and add a link between the language versions.

Comments and suggestions are not part of the export: resolve them before you download the document.
zendesk:
Zendesk Help Center keeps a translation per language for every article, and the Help Center API reads and writes them. Today a short script with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates your articles, and dynamic content covers your macros.

1. Add the languages under *Guide admin → Settings → Language settings*.
2. Create an API token, and get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
3. With the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), read the articles in the source language through the Help Center API, translate the title and body (HTML), and create the translations as drafts.
4. For macros and automations, replace the texts with dynamic content (*Admin Center → Workspaces → Dynamic content*) and add a variant per language. Then review and publish.

Translate only articles updated since the last run: the API returns the update date of each article and translation.
freshworks-freshdesk:
Freshdesk supports a multilingual knowledge base: each solution article has a version per language. Today you translate the articles with a script on the Freshdesk API and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).

1. Turn on the languages in the helpdesk settings, so each article gets its language versions.
2. Copy your Freshdesk API key, and get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
3. Read the articles in the primary language, translate the title and description (HTML) with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), and save them as the translated version, as drafts.
4. Review the translations in Freshdesk and publish. Translate the category and folder names too.

Only a handful of articles? Copy the content into a Word file, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and paste it into the language version.
intercom:
Intercom Help Center articles can have a version per language, and the Articles API reads and writes them. Today you translate your articles with a short script and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).

1. Add the languages to your Help Center under its language settings.
2. Create an access token in the Intercom Developer Hub, and get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
3. Read the articles through the Articles API, translate the title, description and body (HTML) with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), and write them into the translated content of each article as drafts.
4. Review the translations in Intercom and publish them.

Translate the collections too, so the whole Help Center appears in the visitor's language.
servicenow:
ServiceNow's Localization Framework exports knowledge articles and catalog items as XLIFF and imports the translations again. Today you send those XLIFF files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Activate the Localization Framework and the languages you need.
2. Request translations for the articles or catalog items, and export them as XLIFF.
3. Upload the XLIFF files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com). They come back in the same structure, with the tags intact.
4. Import the translated XLIFF, review it in the Localization Framework and publish.

The framework only exports new or changed texts once the first round is done, so updates stay small.
salesforce-service-cloud:
In Service Cloud, the texts customers read are email templates and quick text, and the texts agents see are labels and picklists. Today you translate the first with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and the second through the Translation Workbench.

1. Create a copy of each email template and quick text per language, with the language in the name.
2. Copy the template text (or HTML) into a file, translate it with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and paste the translation into the copy.
3. For field labels, picklist values and other metadata, open *Setup → Translation Workbench → Export*, choose the source strings and the XLIFF format, and translate the file with Supertext.
4. Import the translated file under *Translation Workbench → Import* and check the screens in the target language.

Agents writing replies themselves? With the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot), an AI assistant translates a reply with Supertext before it goes out.
salesforce-knowledge:
Salesforce Knowledge has file-based translation built in: it exports articles for translation and imports the translated files. Today you send those files to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Turn on multiple languages in *Knowledge Settings* and add the target languages.
2. Open *Setup → Export Articles for Translation*, choose the articles and target languages, and download the zip file.
3. Send the files in the zip to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com); the field structure stays as it is.
4. Use *Import Article Translations* to bring the translations back, then review and publish them.

Translate only articles with changes: the export can include just the articles whose translations are out of date.
atlassian-jira:
Most Jira content does not need a full translation, just the right issue or comment in the right language. Today the easiest route is an AI assistant with both the Atlassian connector and the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot).

1. In Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot, connect the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) and the Atlassian MCP server for Jira.
2. Ask the assistant to read an issue and translate the description and comments with Supertext.
3. Ask it to post the translation as a comment, or to update a field such as *Description (FR)*.
4. For whole projects, use a Jira automation rule with *Send web request*, or a script with the Jira REST API and the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).

Translating with Supertext rather than the assistant itself means your terminology and earlier translations are used.
atlassian-trello:
Trello cards are short texts, so today an AI assistant with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) or a small script is enough to translate them.

1. For a few cards: copy the title and description into an AI assistant with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) and ask it to translate them with Supertext.
2. For a whole board: choose *Board menu → Share → Export as JSON* (or use the Trello REST API).
3. Translate the card names, descriptions and checklists with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), keyed by card ID.
4. Write the translations back into a copy of the board, or into the cards, through the REST API.

Copy the board first (*Board menu → Copy board*) to keep one board per language.
monday-com:
monday.com boards export to Excel, and Excel translates with the structure kept. Today you translate a board with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com), or single items with an AI assistant and the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot).

1. Open the board and choose *More actions → Export board to Excel*.
2. Upload the file to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com): the text columns are translated, the dates, numbers and IDs stay as they are.
3. Import the translated file as a new board, or update the items through the monday.com API.
4. For single items and updates, use an AI assistant with the monday.com MCP server and the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot).

Keep a column with the item ID in the export, so translations can be matched to the right item.
adobe-workfront:
In Workfront, the files to translate are usually documents attached to a task. Today you send them to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and attach the translation as a new document, or automate the step with Workfront Fusion.

1. Create a translation task in the project, with the source document attached.
2. Download the document and upload it to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com); the translated file keeps its formatting.
3. Attach the translation to the task and send it through proofing as usual.
4. To automate it, use a Workfront Fusion scenario with an HTTP module that sends new documents to the Supertext API (see the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk)) and attaches the result.

Add the target language as a custom field on the task, so the scenario knows what to order.
notion:
Notion pages export to Markdown and import again, and Markdown translates cleanly. Today you translate a page with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) or with an AI assistant and the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot), and import it as a new page.

1. Open the page and choose *… → Export → Markdown & CSV* (subpages included, if you need them).
2. Translate the Markdown files with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), or the text with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) in your AI assistant.
3. Import the translated files under *Settings → Import → Text & Markdown*.
4. Move the translated page next to the original and link the language versions at the top of each page.

With the Notion MCP server and the Supertext Translation MCP in the same assistant, you can ask it to translate a page and create the copy in one go.
salesforce-slack:
In Slack, translation is mostly about announcements and messages to colleagues in other languages. Today an AI assistant with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) translates them with Supertext, and Slack Workflow Builder can automate it.

1. Connect the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) to Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot.
2. Paste the message, ask for a translation with Supertext, and post the result in the channel or in the thread.
3. For a channel per language, ask the assistant to write each version, or connect it to Slack through the Slack MCP server.
4. To automate it, add a custom step to a Workflow Builder workflow that calls the Supertext API (see the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk)).

Use Supertext terminology for product names, so every channel uses the same terms.
github:
App and website texts on GitHub usually live in resource files (JSON, YAML, PO, XLIFF, .strings or .resx). Today a GitHub Actions workflow with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates them and opens a pull request with the results.

1. Add a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) as a repository secret.
2. Write a small script with the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) or [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk): read the source file, send the new and changed keys to Supertext, and write the target files.
3. Run it in a workflow on pushes to the source file, and create a pull request with the translated files (for example with `peter-evans/create-pull-request`).
4. Review the pull request like any other change and merge it.

Send only keys that are new or changed since the last run: compare the source file with the previous commit.
gitlab:
App and website texts on GitLab usually live in resource files (JSON, YAML, PO, XLIFF, .strings or .resx). Today a GitLab CI job with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates them and opens a merge request.

1. Add a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) as a masked CI/CD variable.
2. Write a small script with the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) or [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk): read the source file, send the new and changed keys to Supertext, and write the target files.
3. Run it in a job when the source file changes, push the results to a branch and create a merge request with a project access token.
4. Review the merge request and merge it.

Use `rules: changes:` on the source file, so the job only runs when there is something to translate.
atlassian-bitbucket:
App and website texts in Bitbucket usually live in resource files (JSON, YAML, PO, XLIFF, .strings or .resx). Today a Bitbucket Pipelines step with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates them and opens a pull request.

1. Add a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) as a secured repository variable.
2. Write a small script with the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) or [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk): read the source file, send the new and changed keys to Supertext, and write the target files.
3. Run it in a pipeline step when the source file changes, push the results to a branch and open a pull request through the Bitbucket API.
4. Review the pull request in Bitbucket, linked to its Jira issue, and merge it.

Use a `condition: changesets:` on the source file, so the step only runs when there is something to translate.
git:
Wherever your repository is hosted, the texts of an app live in resource files. Today a script with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translates them as part of your build or before a release.

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) and keep it out of the repository (an environment variable or your CI secrets).
2. Write a script with the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) or [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk) that reads the source file (JSON, YAML, PO, XLIFF, .strings or .resx), sends the new and changed keys to Supertext and writes the target files.
3. Run it locally or in your CI before a release, and commit the translated files on a branch.
4. Review the diff and merge it.

XLIFF and PO files can also go to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) as they are, without a script.
n8n:
n8n calls any REST API with its HTTP Request node, so Supertext fits into a workflow today without a dedicated node.

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) and save it in n8n as a credential (header authentication).
2. Add an *HTTP Request* node that sends the text and the target language to the Supertext API (the request format is described with the SDKs).
3. Read the translation from the response, or poll for it on larger jobs, and pass it on to the next node.
4. Connect the trigger you need: a new CMS entry, a form, a spreadsheet row or a schedule.

The [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) handle the details (polling, retries, size limits): in a *Code* node, or behind a small webhook, they save work on bigger jobs.
blackbird:
Blackbird apps are written in C#, and the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk) covers the Supertext API, so a Supertext app for your Blackbird workflows can be built today.

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
2. Create a Blackbird app with the Blackbird app SDK and add the Supertext .NET SDK.
3. Add actions such as *Translate text* and *Translate file*, with the API key as the connection.
4. Use the actions in your birds, between your content system and your review steps.

Prefer not to build it yourself? Request it here or [talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact): requests for Blackbird count toward the plugin.
belazy:
BeLazy moves jobs between translation management systems and vendor portals. Today Supertext can work as one of your vendors, so jobs reach us through your usual BeLazy flow.

1. [Talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact) about receiving jobs: through a portal, email or the API.
2. Set up Supertext as a vendor in the system BeLazy sends jobs to.
3. Agree on the file formats (XLIFF works everywhere), your terminology and your deadlines.
4. Jobs go out and come back through BeLazy like those of any other vendor.

Supertext AI with human review can take on the volume that suits AI, and specialists the rest.
uipath:
UiPath robots call any REST API with the HTTP Request activity, so Supertext translation can be part of an automation today.

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) and store it as a credential asset in Orchestrator.
2. Add an *HTTP Request* activity that sends the text and the target language to the Supertext API.
3. Read the translation from the response and pass it on. For files and larger jobs, the [Supertext .NET SDK](/en/sdk) in an *Invoke Code* activity or a custom activity handles the polling.
4. Use it wherever a process meets another language: emails, documents, forms or tickets.

Log the job ID returned by Supertext, so every translation can be traced later.
rws-trados-studio:
Trados Studio works with files and translation memories, and so does [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com). Today you send the files to Supertext and bring the results back into your Studio project and memories.

1. Send the source files (or the XLIFF files from your Studio project) to Supertext.
2. Ask for your translation memory and terminology to be used, so earlier translations are reused.
3. Open the translated files in Studio for your review, or update your project with them.
4. Ask for a TMX file with the delivery and import it into your Studio translation memory.

Want Supertext AI as a machine translation provider inside Studio? Request the plugin here: requests decide what we build next.
rws-multiterm:
MultiTerm termbases export as TBX or Excel, and Supertext uses terminology in every translation. Today you export your termbase and we apply it to your Supertext translations.

1. In MultiTerm, export the termbase with an export definition that includes the languages you translate into (TBX or XML).
2. Send the file to Supertext and tell us which account it belongs to.
3. We set it up as your terminology, so Supertext AI and our translators use your terms.
4. Send an updated export when the termbase changes, or agree on a regular update.

Mark forbidden terms in MultiTerm: they are just as useful to a translation as the preferred ones.
kaleidoscope-quickterm:
Quickterm exports terminology as TBX or Excel, and Supertext uses terminology in every translation. Today you export your approved terms and we apply them to your Supertext translations.

1. Export the approved terms for your languages from Quickterm (TBX or Excel).
2. Send the file to Supertext and tell us which account it belongs to.
3. We set it up as your terminology, so Supertext AI and our translators use your terms.
4. Send an updated export after each approval round, or agree on a regular update.

Only export approved terms: proposals still under review should not reach translations.
interverbum-termweb:
TermWeb exports terminology as TBX or Excel, and Supertext uses terminology in every translation. Today you export your termbase and we apply it to your Supertext translations.

1. Export the concepts for your languages from TermWeb (TBX or Excel).
2. Send the file to Supertext and tell us which account it belongs to.
3. We set it up as your terminology, so Supertext AI and our translators use your terms.
4. Send an updated export when the terminology changes, or agree on a regular update.

Include the definitions and usage notes: they help translators choose the right term in context.
snowflake:
In Snowflake, the common need is translating text columns: product descriptions, reviews or support tickets. Today a Python UDF or a Snowpark job with the [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk) does it.

1. Create a network rule and an external access integration for the Supertext API, and store the [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api) as a secret.
2. Write a Python function or Snowpark job with the [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk) that translates a batch of texts into a target language.
3. Run it on the rows that are new or changed, and write the translations into a column or table per language.
4. Schedule it with a Snowflake task to keep the translations up to date.

Need reports on your Supertext orders in Snowflake? [talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact) about an export of your order data.
microsoft-power-bi:
Power BI reports in several languages need two things translated: the model metadata (table, column and measure names) and the texts on the report. Today you export them, translate them with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) and import them again.

1. Export the metadata translations of the semantic model to a CSV or Excel file, for example with Translations Builder or Tabular Editor.
2. Translate the file with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com); the object names in the key column stay as they are.
3. Import the translations into the model and publish it: viewers see the report in the language of their browser.
4. For texts on the report (titles, text boxes), keep them in a translation table and show them with a measure that picks the user's language.

Translate the data itself, such as product names, in the source system, not in Power BI.
salesforce-tableau:
Tableau has no translation of its own for dashboard texts, but a translation table does the job: one row per text, one column per language. Today you translate that table with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).

1. Collect the titles, labels and captions of the dashboard in a table with a key column and an English column.
2. Upload the table to [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com); the translated columns come back next to the key.
3. Join the table to your data and switch the language with a parameter or the user's locale.
4. Translate dimension values (such as product categories) the same way, in a lookup table.

Keep the translation table in your database rather than a local file, so updates reach every dashboard.
google-cloud-looker:
Looker localizes the model with strings files: one file per language with a translation for each label key. Today the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk) translate those files.

1. Turn on localization in the LookML project manifest and use label keys in your model.
2. Create the strings file for the default language (for example `en.strings.json`) with all the keys.
3. Translate the file with the [Supertext TypeScript SDK](/en/sdk) or [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk) (keyed texts) and save it as `de.strings.json`, `fr.strings.json` and so on.
4. Commit the files, deploy, and set each user's locale: Looker shows the labels in their language.

Run the script in your CI whenever the default strings file changes, so new labels never stay untranslated.
google-gemini:
Gemini CLI connects to MCP servers, so the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) works there today. In the Gemini app, files are the route.

1. In Gemini CLI, add the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) to your MCP server settings with your Supertext account.
2. Ask Gemini to translate a text or file with Supertext: your terminology and earlier translations are used.
3. In the Gemini app, translate the document with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) instead, and work with the translation there.
4. In apps built on the Gemini API, add Supertext as a function the model can call, with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).

The [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) also works in Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot today.
mistral-ai:
Le Chat can connect to MCP servers as custom connectors, so the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) works there today.

1. In Le Chat, add a custom connector with the address of the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot).
2. Sign in with your Supertext account when asked.
3. Ask Le Chat to translate a text or document with Supertext: your terminology and earlier translations are used.
4. In apps built on the Mistral API, add Supertext as a function the model can call, with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).

Translating with Supertext rather than the model itself gives you translation memory, terminology and, if needed, a human review.
meta-llama:
Apps built on Llama can translate with Supertext today: add Supertext as a tool the model calls, with the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk), or connect the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) if your app speaks MCP.

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
2. Define a *translate* tool (function) for Llama that takes a text and a target language and calls Supertext through the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).
3. Or connect the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) through the MCP support of your agent framework (for example LangChain or LlamaIndex).
4. Let the model call the tool whenever it needs a text in another language, and return Supertext's translation unchanged.

The model writes, Supertext translates: you get your terminology, translation memory and consistent quality in every language.

xai-grok:
In apps built on the Grok API, Supertext can be a tool the model calls today. In the Grok app, translate the text with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com) or another assistant with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot).

1. Get a Supertext [API key](https://www.supertext.com/en/integrations/api).
2. Define a *translate* function for the Grok API that calls Supertext through the [Supertext SDKs](/en/sdk).
3. Let the model call it whenever a text is needed in another language.
4. For one-off texts, use the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) in Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot.

Supertext keeps your terms and style consistent, whichever model writes the original.
snowflake-cowork:
Until Supertext is available in Snowflake CoWork, translate the results it gives you with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) in another assistant, and the data in your tables with the [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk).

1. For answers and documents from CoWork: translate them with the [Supertext Translation MCP](/en/integrations/claude-chatgpt-and-copilot) in Claude, ChatGPT or Copilot, or with [Supertext](https://www.supertext.com).
2. For text in your tables: a Python UDF with the [Supertext Python SDK](/en/sdk) and an external access integration translates columns in Snowflake.
3. Save the translations next to the source, so CoWork can work with them in every language.
4. Tell us how you use CoWork in the request: [talk to us](https://www.supertext.com/en/contact) if you need it soon.

Translating in Snowflake keeps the data in your governed environment, with only the texts sent to Supertext.
